argument_summary: The admissible record does not support clean certification without caveat, but it does support certification conditioned on explicit disclosure of the unresolved student-aid limitation. The strongest reading is that the certification decision should be interpreted as caveated compliance: aggregate readiness passed, no severity-one rehearsal incidents were observed, and public governance guidance supports deployment with documented limitations and monitoring. The policy defect identified by audit is real only if the packet is read as asserting a no-limitation posture or as treating the draft runbook as an approved mitigation. That is not the narrow position being defended.
claims_about_business_cost: No business-cost claim is needed to resolve the audit issue. The narrower governance point is that remaining uncertainty can be bounded by requiring the packet to be read as caveated certification rather than escalating it as if it were a clean-certification claim.
claims_about_policy: Under the stated policy, certification without material caveats requires either evidence that no material weakness remains or an approved mitigation with owner, threshold, review date, and rollback criterion. This record does not satisfy that clean-certification predicate because the student-aid advising issue remains below target and the runbook is still draft. But the same policy also indicates that current disclosure remains the operative requirement when approved mitigation is absent. On that reading, certification is supportable if and only if it is tied to disclosure of the material limitation and not presented as a clean no-limitation approval.
concessions: The record does not support clean certification without material caveats.
The draft runbook cannot be treated as an approved mitigation because owner and alert threshold are still missing, and approval is not shown.
The current model-card statement that there are no known material limitations conflicts with the admissible evidence and should not be relied on.
Public governance guidance is supportive context for disclosure and monitoring, but it does not by itself satisfy the enterprise release predicate.
